In [[mathematics]], '''Young functions''' are a class of functions that arise in [[functional analysis]], especially in the study of [[Orlicz space]]s.

== Definition ==

A function <math>\theta : \R \to [0, \infty]</math> is called a ''Young function'' if it is [[Convex function|convex]], [[Even function|even]], [[Semi-continuity|lower semicontinuous]], and non-trivial, in the sense that it is neither the zero function <math>x \mapsto 0</math> nor its convex dual

:<math>x \mapsto \begin{cases} \,\,\,0 & \text{ if } x = 0, \\ +\infty & \text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}</math>

A Young function said to be ''finite'' if it does not take the value <math>\infty</math>.

A Young function <math>\theta</math> is ''strict'' if both <math>\theta</math> and its [[Convex conjugate|convex dual]] <math>\theta^*</math> are finite; i.e.,  

:<math>\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\theta(x)} x = \infty.</math>

The inverse of a Young function is given by <math>\theta^{-1}(y)=\inf \{x: \theta(x)>y\}</math>.

Some authors (such as Krasnosel'skii and Rutickii){{Citation needed|date=October 2025}} also require that 

:<math>\lim_{x \downarrow 0} \frac{\theta(x)}{x} = 0</math>.

=== Norm ===

Let <math>\mu</math> be a [[σ-finite measure]] on a set <math>X</math>, and <math>\theta</math> a Young function. For any [[measurable function|measurable]] function <math>f</math> on <math>X</math>, we define the ''Luxemburg'' norm as

:<math>\|f\|_\theta = \inf\left\{b>0\;\bigg\vert\int_X \theta(|f|/b)\,d\mu\le 1 \right\}.</math>

== Examples ==

The following functions are Young functions:

* <math>\theta_\text{exp}(x) = e^{|x|} - 1</math>.

* <math>\theta_p(x) = |s|^p/p</math> for all <math>p\geq 1</math>. This function leads to the usual norm <math>p^{1/p}\|f\|_\theta=\|f\|_p = (\textstyle\int_X |f|^p d\mu)^{1/p}</math> on <math>L^p(\mu)</math>.
